catalog_quote: 1.4. Stress. Stress has a purely delimitative function in Gunin: no two words are distinguished by placement of stress. It is entirely predictable, and always falls on the initial syllable of a word. This holds irrespective of the 'size' of the initial syllable. Thus, if the initial syllable is a vowel, it is still stressed, as in 'amaarr 'bone of an animal', 'aarru 'stone' ... If a simple root has more than three syllables, there is usually another stressed syllable in addition to the first. This is the third syllable, as in: 'galamamda 'paddle'; 'girranggarlu 'brolga'; and ngarringurdugal 'apple'. As these examples show, the second stressed syllable is usually somewhat less stressed than the first. If the root has two or three syllables, only the first syllable is normally stressed. However, some trisyllabic simple roots do bear stress on their third syllable, especially if it is closed. ... Each reduplicated formative or morpheme is separately stressed, as though it were a separate unit. ... Both pitch and length are independent of stress. ... And whereas in some Aboriginal languages long syllables attract stress -- e.g. Gooniyandi (McGregor 1990:121-123) -- this does not hold in Gunin. Short and long syllables may equally be stressed. For instance, the first syllable of 'amaarr 'bone of animal' is stressed even though it consists of a single short vowel and the following syllable is not only closed, but consists of a long vowel.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of every word, with no weight sensitivity: an initial syllable consisting of a bare short vowel is stressed even when the next syllable is closed and long (e.g. 'amaarr 'bone of an animal', 'aarru 'stone'), unlike Gooniyandi where long syllables attract stress. Stress never distinguishes words (purely delimitative). Simple roots of four or more syllables usually add a weaker second stress on the third syllable; roots of two or three syllables normally have only the initial stress. Pitch and vowel length are independent of stress; the high central vowel is always stressed in initial syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In simple (non-reduplicated) roots of more than three syllables a second, weaker stress usually falls on the third syllable ('galamarnda, 'girranggarlu, ngarringurdugal); some trisyllabic simple roots also bear a second stress (sentence truncated in the snippets). Reduplicated units are each stressed 'irrespective of the number of syllables in the reduplicated unit, and whether reduplication is partial [or complete]' (p. 19).
new_statements.exceptions: None to initial primary stress ('entirely predictable'); explicitly no long-syllable attraction. The only qualification concerns the second stress: 'some trisyllabic simple roots do bear [a second stress]' (continuation not recovered). Pitch is not a reliable correlate: a stressed syllable 'may be higher pitched than a neighbouring unstressed syllable, [but] this is not invariably' so.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (the initial syllable 'of a word'); rule stated for simple roots and reduplications; stress placement is also used on pp. 19-21 as evidence for syllabifying consonant sequences. Nothing recovered about clitics, prefixed verbs or phrase-level prominence. Data are McGregor's own Kalumburu fieldwork plus Capell's 1930s corpus (per the sketch's introduction snippets).
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes Gunin, the language of the Kwini people of Kalumburu (McGregor 1993:5: 'Gunin is the name of the language, while Kwini (['g@wiini]) [is the people]'); AIATSIS K36; ISO gww; matches kwin1241. Northern Worrorran together with Wunambal (wuna1254), Gaambera, Miwa, Wilawila and Yiiji (McGregor & Rumsey 2009:8). Tindale conflated it with Miwa (K44) and Jones 2006 lumps it with Yiiji/Wunambal as 'Forrest River language'; McGregor keeps Gunin separate. The Wunambal stress rule in Carr 2001 (penultimate primary in longer words) differs from the Gunin rule and must not be merged.

sources.note: Wunambal (wuna1254), not Kwini -- the closest relative. Sec. 2.4 Stress p. 61: 'In words of more than 3 syllables primary stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable, and secondary stress on the first syllable'; disyllables and most trisyllables stressed on the first syllable; 4-syllable words initial primary + secondary on 3rd/penult; suffixes/postpositions carry their own stress; fn. 21 loudness taken as the cue, length-stress interaction unresolved. Ch. 1 treats Kwini as a separate closely related variety and cites McGregor (1993) as its sketch grammar.
